history.note: Egyptians measured the Nile's flood with graduated stairs and wells to forecast harvests and set taxes.
Greek drinking parties where men debated, recited poetry and argued philosophy; Plato set a dialogue at one.
Tea drinking spread across China under the Tang; Lu Yu's 'Classic of Tea' (8th century) codified its preparation.

name: Coffeehouse
description: +2 culture in settlements with 2+ trade routes.

history.note: Coffeehouses spread from Yemen to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul in the 15th–16th centuries as places for news, poetry and debate.
Free men met at the thing to settle disputes and make law. Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, met at Þingvellir for centuries, and Iceland's parliament still bears its name.

name: Qajaq
description: Naval units +2 movement in polar and boreal waters.

history.note: The qajaq, a skin-covered hunting boat built to each paddler's body, gave the English word 'kayak'.
The ger, a felt tent on a collapsible lattice frame, can be taken down and moved in hours; many Mongolians still live in one.
history.source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Traditional craftsmanship of the Mongol Ger and its associated customs'

name: Siesta
description: +2 happiness in arid and tropical settlements.

history.note: A midday rest during the hottest hours, from the Latin 'hora sexta', the sixth hour after dawn.
Large landed estates of Spain and its empire. In the Americas many relied on coerced Indigenous labor and debt peonage that bound workers for generations.
Each year at Thebes the images of Amun, Mut and Khonsu travelled by river barge and in procession from Karnak to Luxor temple, a feast that renewed the king's divine power before the crowds.
While the flood covered the fields, the state called farmers up for building work. The Giza pyramid crews were fed, housed and organised in gangs, not enslaved, but the labor duty was compulsory.
history.source: Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass, Giza and the Pyramids (2017)

history.note: The per-ankh, or House of Life, was a temple workshop where scribes copied and kept religious, medical and astronomical texts and trained new scribes.
history.source: Alan H. Gardiner, 'The House of Life', Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 24 (1938)

name: Pyramid builders
description: Wonders cost 20% less; +20% production in the capital.

history.note: In the Old Kingdom (c. 2600–2500 BCE) the state gathered food, stone and many thousands of workers to raise the pyramids of Sneferu, Khufu and Khafre; the Great Pyramid stayed the tallest building on Earth for some 3,800 years.
From the 4th century Coptic Christians founded desert monasteries, from St Antony's to Pachomius's communities at Tabennisi, whose rules of shared work and prayer became models for monks everywhere.
From 776 BCE by tradition, Greeks from rival cities gathered every four years at Olympia for games in honor of Zeus, under a sacred truce that let athletes and visitors travel safely.
From the 8th to 6th centuries BCE Greek cities sent out settlers to found colonies from Spain to the Black Sea, often taking land from the peoples already living there.
Citizen-soldiers who bought their own round shield and spear fought shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx; fighting for the city went hand in hand with a say in its government.

Athenian democracy (from 508/507 BCE) let citizens vote in the Assembly and serve by lot on juries and councils. Citizenship was limited to adult men of Athenian birth; women, foreigners and the enslaved were excluded.
Since at least the Shang, Chinese families have made offerings to ancestors whose favor was believed to guard the lineage; Shang kings put questions to royal ancestors through oracle bones.

The Zhou justified overthrowing the Shang (c. 1046 BCE) by claiming that Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and takes it from tyrants, an idea later used to explain every change of dynasty.

In 119 BCE Emperor Wu of Han made salt and iron state monopolies to pay for his wars on the Xiongnu. A court debate in 81 BCE, the Discourses on Salt and Iron, pitted his officials against Confucian scholars.

From the Sui and Tang, and fully under the Song, officials were chosen by written exams on the Confucian classics. Open in principle to most men, they favored families who could afford years of study; women were barred.
Domesticated in Arabia by about 1000 BCE, the dromedary could go days without water, opening Arabia's deserts to long-distance caravans and to herding peoples such as the Qedarites.
Before Islam, Arab tribes met each year at the fair of ʿUkāẓ near Ṭāʾif, under a sacred truce, to trade and hold poetry contests; tradition links the finest odes, the Muʿallaqāt, to it.
Frankincense and myrrh from South Arabia went by caravan through oases such as Najrān, Dedan and Taymāʾ to Gaza and Damascus, enriching the peoples who held the wells and tolls along the way.

name: Waqf
description: +1 happiness in settlements of 5+ population; +10% faith.

history.note: A waqf was a charitable endowment: income from land or shops given in perpetuity to fund mosques, schools, hospitals, fountains and the poor. Waqfs shaped Islamic cities for over a thousand years.

The House of Wisdom in Abbasid Baghdad (9th century) was a palace library and translation centre under caliphs such as al-Maʾmūn, drawing scholars of many faiths and origins. Its exact size and role are debated.
In the Nordic Bronze Age, amber from Jutland and the Baltic went south across Europe in exchange for copper and tin; Scandinavia's rich bronzes were cast from metal it had to import.
history.source: National Museum of Denmark, 'The Bronze Age'

history.note: Skalds composed intricate praise poems for kings and chieftains, dense with kennings. Icelandic skalds served at Norwegian courts, and their verses were later quoted as historical evidence.
Under the leiðangr, districts had to build, crew and supply warships for the king's levy, a system that organised Scandinavian sea defence from the late Viking Age into the 13th century.

name: Landnám (land-taking)
description: Settlement cap +1; +1 food on boreal tiles.

history.note: From the 9th century Norse settlers took land in the Faroes, Iceland and Greenland, recorded farm by farm in Iceland's Landnámabók. They brought livestock and also enslaved Irish and British captives.

name: Longships
description: Naval units +2 movement and +4 combat strength.

history.note: Fast under sail or oar and shallow enough to row far up rivers, longships carried traders and settlers, and raiders who plundered monasteries and towns and carried off captives to sell.
history.source: Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo, 'The Viking Ship Museum'

name: Sharing the catch
description: +1 food in polar and boreal settlements.

history.note: Inuit custom shares a hunter's catch across the camp by set rules of who receives which part, so that no household goes hungry while others eat.
Katajjaq is a vocal game in which two women face each other and trade quick rhythmic sounds until one laughs or runs out of breath. Missionaries discouraged it; it has since revived.

name: Umialik whaling crews
description: +1 food on fish; naval units +3 combat strength.

history.note: An umialik, owner and captain of a large skin boat, led a crew hunting bowhead whales. One whale could feed a community through the winter, and its meat was shared out by custom.

name: Qamutiik (dog sled)
description: Units +1 movement on snow and tundra.

history.note: The qamutiik, a sled of wood or bone runners lashed with sinew and drawn by a fan-hitched team of dogs, let Inuit families move camp and haul loads over sea ice and snow.

name: Iglu (snow house)
description: No cold penalties; +1 food on snow and tundra.

history.note: Snow houses let Inuit live out on the sea ice through winter, close to the seals' breathing holes. Built from blocks of wind-packed snow, an iglu stays far warmer inside than the air outside.
Steppe herders milk mares and ferment the milk into airag (kumis). Milk proteins in ancient dental calculus show horse milking in Mongolia by about 1200 BCE, and airag is still drunk every summer.
history.source: Shevan Wilkin et al., 'Dairy pastoralism sustained eastern Eurasian steppe populations for 5,000 years', Nature Ecology & Evolution 4 (2020)

history.note: Mongolian herders move between seasonal pastures, often four times a year, so grass can recover. Mobile herding of horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels has sustained steppe life for three thousand years.
The khuriltai was the assembly of Mongol princes and commanders that chose khans and decided on war; Temüjin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan at one by the Onon River in 1206.
Chinggis Khan organised his army in units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, deliberately mixing men of different tribes to break old loyalties; the system made Mongol armies disciplined and hard to stop.

Riding from childhood, steppe warriors shot composite bows from the saddle and rode with several remounts each. Feigned retreats and encirclement beat larger armies across Eurasia, at terrible cost to the conquered.

Silver from the Río Tinto and other south-western Iberian mines drew Phoenician and Greek traders to Tartessos from the 9th century BCE. Rome later worked the same mines on a vast scale with enslaved and convict labor.
The falcata, a curved, single-edged sword used by Iberian warriors from about the 5th century BCE, was prized for its cutting power; Roman writers admired the quality of Iberian steel.
history.source: Fernando Quesada Sanz, Armas de la antigua Iberia (2010)

history.note: Chartered by Alfonso X in 1273, the Mesta was a royal guild of sheep owners whose flocks walked the cañadas between summer and winter pastures. Wool became Castile's great export, often at farmers' expense.
Iberian kings granted fueros, local charters of rights and laws, to frontier towns to draw settlers into lands taken from al-Andalus, whose Muslim inhabitants were often expelled or made subjects.

name: Land of castles
description: Units +5 combat strength on hills; an extra Marshal seat.

history.note: Castile took its name from the castles guarding its frontier with al-Andalus. Military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago held these fortresses through centuries of war, raiding and conquest.
